extracted.intended_audience: general readers and speakers interested in comic/occasional speech and humorous writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative principles for crafting public humorous addresses and comic prose, drawn from Mark Twain's banquet and public speeches. Focuses on rhetorical devices, language choices, and audience-aware comedic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exaggeration/hyperbole as a primary comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: "To exaggerate is the only way I can approximate to the truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain repeatedly uses overstatement to make points funnier and more memorable (e.g., imagining half a crown costing $10,000, saying Carnegie's simplified spelling "brought destruction to the entire race"). Exaggeration can be presented as literal misunderstanding or absurd scale to produce humor and to caricature subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and simplicity of vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer short, simple words; avoid long, pretentious terms when plain ones will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain gives a practical and rhetorical argument: language should be concise and economical (anecdote about being paid seven cents a word—using 'city' instead of 'metropolis', 'cop' instead of 'policeman'). Guidance includes shaving vocabulary to three- or four-letter averages to increase clarity, speed, and comic punch; long multisyllabic words are presented as obstacles to both comedy and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language's essential function: convey ideas and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is the real function, the essential function, the supreme function, of language? Isn't it merely to convey ideas and emotions? Certainly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whatever linguistic forms most effectively transmit thought and feeling. If shorter, phonetic, or simplified forms convey the idea better (and more amusingly), they are preferable. This principle underpins arguments for plain wording and phonetic play in comic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal anecdote and vivid storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrate points with personal stories and concrete incidents (e.g., the Atlantic bet/half-crown story, printing-office reminiscences, the editor with the long technical text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes provide grounding, set up absurdity, and create rapport with the audience. Twain models building humor by telling a believable-seeming mini-story and then delivering an unexpected punch or moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecation and ironic acceptance of compliments
rubrics_metrics.description: Feigning delight in compliments while undercutting them with self-revelation or mock threats (e.g., saying he enjoys compliments but might use a gun on a chairman next time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix genuine-sounding gratitude with ironic aside or contradiction to create tension and laughter. Presenting both the praise and the 'other side' (wickedness, interior sin) allows comic contrast and humane humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical comparisons and absurd analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sharp, often grotesque analogies to lampoon subjects (e.g., likening Carnegie's spelling reform to Torquemada and the Inquisition; calling the alphabet 'invented by a drunken thief').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bold comparisons that stretch logic but convey emotional truth can create striking comic effect. The comparison should be vivid, optionally historically or culturally exaggerated, to highlight folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay, phonetic humor, and playful orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with spelling and sound for humorous effect and to make a point about language (Twain's advocacy and comic demonstrations for 'simplified spelling' and 'fonetic brevity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate misspelling, phonetic spellings, and mock-technical language can be used both as satire and as a device to speed rhythm, create surprise, or lampoon pedantry. Twain uses invented polysyllables and mock-Latin compounds as targets of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ surprise and reversal in rhetorical arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up expected courtesy or a conventional statement and then reverse or escalate it (e.g., many compliments followed by a comic threat to use a gun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build audience expectation with conventional material, then pivot to an incongruous or extreme reaction to produce a laugh. Timing and placement of the reversal are critical—often delivered as an aside or conjunction after a string of conventional praises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be audience- and context-aware
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust content for occasion, social norms, and timing (e.g., refraining from certain histrionics 'in public' or 'too near Sunday').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor jokes to the setting: what is allowable at a press dinner, a club banquet, or a religiously sensitive evening may differ. References to local institutions and topical events (Galveston disaster, Carnegie, Associated Press) increase relevance but require sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony to puncture pretension and critique 'serious' literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the self-important or supposedly solemn as comedic targets (e.g., classics that 'everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read'; mocking critics' claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony—saying the opposite of what is meant, or framing a grand claim in a trivial light—exposes affectation and invites the audience to share an inside joke about cultural pretensions.
